content.title: Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves
content.overview: Arc length represents the total distance traveled by a particle along a path in a plane. For curves defined by parametric equations or vector-valued functions, the arc length is calculated by integrating the speed of the particle over a specified time interval.
learning_objectives: Define the arc length formula for parametric and vector-valued functions.
Identify the relationship between speed and the integrand of the arc length formula.
Set up and evaluate definite integrals to find the distance traveled along a curve.
Apply the arc length formula to functions defined analytically or through numerical data.

sections.title: The Arc Length Formula
sections.content:
For a curve defined parametrically by x = f(t) and y = g(t), or by the vector-valued function r(t) = <f(t), g(t)>, the arc length S from t = a to t = b is given by the integral of the magnitude of the velocity vector. Mathematically, S = ∫[a, b] √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt. This formula assumes that the derivatives dx/dt and dy/dt are continuous on the interval [a, b] and that the curve is traversed exactly once.

![A flow chart showing the steps: 1. Differentiate x(t) and y(t). 2. Square the derivatives. 3. Sum the squares and take the square root. 4. Integrate over the interval a, b.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/d7d70b5e-093a-4737-b41b-926a9af61171-1786526322238-559.webp)

sections.title: Connection to Speed
sections.content: In the context of motion, the expression √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) represents the speed of the particle at time t. Therefore, the arc length is the definite integral of speed with respect to time. This is consistent with the fundamental principle that distance equals the accumulation of speed over a time interval.

sections.title: Vector-Valued Notation
sections.content: When working with a vector-valued function r(t), the derivative r'(t) represents the velocity vector <x'(t), y'(t)>. The arc length is the integral of the norm (magnitude) of the velocity vector: S = ∫[a, b] ||r'(t)|| dt. This notation is functionally identical to the parametric form but is often used in vector calculus contexts.

worked_examples.question: A particle moves along a path defined by the parametric equations x(t) = 3t² and y(t) = 2t³ for the time interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Set up and evaluate the integral for the total distance traveled by the particle.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find the derivatives of the components. dx/dt = 6t and dy/dt = 6t². Step 2: Set up the arc length integral. S = ∫[0, 1] √((6t)² + (6t²)²) dt = ∫[0, 1] √(36t² + 36t⁴) dt. Step 3: Simplify the integrand. S = ∫[0, 1] √(36t²(1 + t²)) dt = ∫[0, 1] 6t√(1 + t²) dt. Step 4: Use u-substitution. Let u = 1 + t², then du = 2t dt, or 3 du = 6t dt. When t=0, u=1; when t=1, u=2. Step 5: Evaluate. S = ∫[1, 2] 3√u du = [2u^(3/2)] from 1 to 2 = 2(2√2 - 1) = 4√2 - 2.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to square the derivatives inside the square root.
Confusing the arc length formula with the surface area formula (which includes an extra factor of 2πy or 2πx).
Integrating the components x(t) and y(t) directly instead of their derivatives.
Neglecting to check if the curve is traced more than once over the given interval, which would lead to an overestimation of the physical length.
exam_tips: If the integral looks impossible to solve by hand on the Calculator section, use the numerical integration function on your graphing calculator.
Always verify that the limits of integration correspond to the parameter t, not the coordinates x or y.
Remember that 'total distance traveled' and 'arc length' are synonymous for these types of curves.
content.recap: The arc length of a parametric or vector curve is the integral of the speed, calculated as the square root of the sum of the squares of the component derivatives over a specific interval of the parameter t.

knowledge_claims.content: The arc length S of a parametric curve from t = a to t = b is defined as the integral from a to b of √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt.
The integrand in the arc length formula, √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²), represents the instantaneous speed of a particle moving along the curve.
Arc length for a parametric curve is equivalent to the total distance traveled by a particle along that path over the given time interval.
To find the arc length of a vector-valued function r(t), one must integrate the magnitude of the velocity vector, ||r'(t)||, with respect to t.
The arc length formula requires that the derivatives of the parametric equations, x'(t) and y'(t), are continuous on the interval of integration.
A common error is failing to square the derivatives, resulting in the incorrect integrand √(dx/dt + dy/dt).
If a problem asks for the 'total distance traveled' by a particle with position <x(t), y(t)>, the arc length integral should be used.
When evaluating arc length, ensure the limits of integration are values of the parameter t, not x or y coordinates.
For a vector function r(t) = <f(t), g(t)>, the arc length is calculated as ∫ ||<f'(t), g'(t)>|| dt.
The velocity vector of a parametric path is defined as v(t) = <x'(t), y'(t)>, and its magnitude is the speed used in arc length calculations.
The arc length integral accumulates small segments of linear distance, ds = √(dx² + dy²), along the curve.
Integrating the speed over an interval where the curve retraces its path will result in the total distance traveled, which may exceed the geometric length of the static curve.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves: Arc length accumulates speed, using the square root of the sum of squared component derivatives.
options.B: Alternating Series and Error: An alternating series converges when magnitudes decrease to zero, and its truncation error is bounded by the first omitted magnitude.
options.C: Infinite Limits and Asymptotes: Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies.
options.D: Derivatives of Inverse Functions: The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Arc length accumulates speed, using the square root of the sum of squared component derivatives. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Ratio and Root Tests: Ratio and root limits below one imply absolute convergence and above one imply divergence, while a limit of one is inconclusive.
options.B: Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves: Arc length accumulates speed, using the square root of the sum of squared component derivatives.
options.C: Derivative as a Limit: The derivative is the limit of average rates of change and represents instantaneous rate of change or tangent-line slope.
options.D: Exponential, Logarithmic, and Inverse Trigonometric Derivatives: Standard derivatives for exponential, logarithmic, and inverse trigonometric functions combine with product, quotient, and chain rules.
